[[File:Arrows in Okazaki.jpeg|300px|thumb|right|Advertising [[billboards]] in [[Okazaki, Aichi|Okazaki]], Japan, featuring many different arrow symbols]]

An '''arrow''' is a graphical [[symbol]], such as ←, ↑, ↓ or →, or a [[pictogram]], used to point or indicate direction. In its simplest form, an arrow is a [[triangle]], [[Chevron (insignia)|chevron]], or [[Kite (geometry)#Characterizations|concave kite]], usually
affixed to a [[line segment]] or [[rectangle]],<ref name="Design Arrows">{{Cite web |url=https://www.travelwayfinding.com/design-arrows-wayfinding-signage/ |title=How to Design and Use Arrows on Signage for Wayfinding |website=Travel wayfinding |date=7 April 2019 |at=Key Point 5; Key Point 9 |access-date=17 July 2019}}</ref> and in more complex forms a representation of an actual [[arrow]] (e.g., ➵ U+27B5). The direction indicated by an arrow is the one along the length of the line or rectangle toward the single pointed end.

==History==
An older (medieval) convention is the [[manicule]] (pointing hand, ☚).
[[Pedro Reinel]] in {{circa|1505}} first used the [[fleur-de-lis]] as indicating north in a [[compass rose]]; 
the convention of marking the eastern direction with a cross is older (medieval).<ref>''The American Revolution, 1775-1783: An Atlas of 18th Century Maps and Charts, Theatres of Operations'', United States  Naval History Division (1972), [https://books.google.com/books?id=VYdCpYUAchYC&pg=PA14  14f.]</ref>

Use of the arrow symbol does not appear to pre-date the 18th century. An early arrow symbol is found in an illustration of [[Bernard Forest de Bélidor]]'s treatise ''L'architecture hydraulique'', printed in France in 1737. The arrow is here used to illustrate the direction of the flow of water and of the water wheel's rotation. At about the same time, arrow symbols were used to indicate the flow of rivers in maps.<ref>E. H. Dobrich, "Pictorial Instructions" in: H. Barlow et al. (eds.), ''Images and understanding'', Cambridge University Press (1990).</ref>

A trend toward abstraction, in which the arrow's [[fletching]] is removed, can be observed in the mid-to-late 19th century. The arrow can be seen in the work of [[Paul Klee]]. In a further refinement of the symbol, John Richard Green's ''[[A Short History of the English People]]'' of 1874 contained maps by cartographer Emil Reich, which indicated army movements by curved lines, with solid triangular arrowheads placed intermittently along the lines.<ref name=APHS2015>[https://printinghistory.org/arrow/ History of the Arrow], American Printing History Society (2015).</ref>

==Main usage==
[[File:Fire exit.svg|thumb|right|An [[exit sign]] with an arrow to indicate the exit is to the left]]
{{Expand section|date=July 2019}}
Arrows are universally recognised for indicating directions.<ref name="Design Arrows" /> They are widely used on [[signage]] and for [[wayfinding]],<ref name="Design Arrows" /> and are often used in [[road surface marking]]s.
A [[two-way road]] may be indicated by "↕" or "⇅".

==In mathematics and sciences==
Upward arrows are often used to indicate an increase in a numerical value, and downward arrows indicate a decrease.

In [[mathematical logic]], a right-facing arrow indicates [[material conditional]], and a left-right (bidirectional) arrow indicates [[if and only if]], an upwards arrow indicates the [[NAND operator]] (negation of conjunction), an downwards arrow indicates the [[logical NOR|NOR operator]] (negation of disjunction).

Use of arrow symbols in [[mathematical notation]] developed in the first half of the 20th century.<ref>Green, J.J, Rossberg, M., and Ebert, P.A., : ''The Convenience of the Typesetter; Notation and Typography in Frege’s Grundgesetze der Arithmetik'', Bulletin of Symbolic Logic 21 (2015): 13–30, fn. 17 [http://soliton.vm.bytemark.co.uk/pub/jjg/pdf/cott.pdf] | [https://dx.doi.org/10.1017/bsl.2015.5 DOI]</ref> 
[[David Hilbert]] in 1922 introduced the arrow symbol representing [[material conditional|logical implication]]. 
The double-headed arrow representing [[logical equivalence]] was introduced by Albrecht Becker in ''Die Aristotelische Theorie der Möglichkeitsschlüsse'', Berlin, 1933.<ref name=APHS2015/>

[[Knuth's up-arrow notation]] uses multiple up arrows, such as ⇈, for iterated, or repeated, exponentiation (''[[tetration]]'').

The quantum theory of [[electron spin]] uses either upward or downward arrows.

A [[vector (mathematics and physics)|vector]] may be denoted with an overhead arrow, such as in <math>\vec{x}</math> or <math display=inline>\stackrel \longrightarrow{AB}</math>.

Some computer programming languages, like Haskell, use [[arrow (computer science)|arrows]] (typed as ->) to denote a type class.

In chemistry, arrows indicate a chemical reaction. For example, {{chem|2H<sub>2</sub> + O<sub>2</sub> → 2H<sub>2</sub>O}} shows that hydrogen and oxygen react to produce water.

==Graffiti==
Arrows are regularly used in contemporary [[graffiti]] designs, incorporated as an element in both simplistic [[Tag (graffiti)|tags]] and complex [[wildstyle]] [[Piece (graffiti)|pieces]]. Arrows are used as a visual technique to make a graffito stand out or give it a sense of movement.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Spiegel |first1=Ilyse |title=The History and Evolution of Arrows in Graffiti Art |url=https://panic39.com/en-gb/blogs/news/the-history-and-evolution-of-arrows-in-graffiti-art |website=panic39.com |date=22 May 2022}}</ref> The graffiti theoretician [[Rammellzee|RAMM:ΣLL:ZΣΣ]] described adornments, such as arrows, in [[wildstyle]] paintings as ornaments that ‘armed’ the letters of a piece.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Gopinath |first1=Gabrielle |editor1-last=Lovata |editor1-first=Troy |editor2-last=Olton |editor2-first=Elizabeth |title=Understanding Graffiti: Multidisciplinary Studies from Prehistory to the Present |date=2015 |publisher=[[Left Coast Press]] |location=United States of America |isbn=978-1-61132-868-4 |page=126 |chapter=Ornament as Armament: Playing Defence in Wildstyle Graffiti}}</ref> The [[Philadelphia]] graffiti artist Cool Earl began using arrows in 1967,<ref>{{cite web |last1=Pope |first1=Alex |last2=Riva |first2=Giulia ‘BLocal’ |title=History of graffiti and street art: the 1960s and the 1970s |url=https://straatmuseum.com/en/blog/history-of-graffiti-and-street-art-1960s-1970s |website=[[STRAAT Museum]] |date=1 April 2021}}</ref> although the New York graffiti writer [[SJK 171]] may have been the first to do so.<ref>{{cite web |title=About |url=https://www.sjk171.com/about.html |website=sjk171.com}}</ref> The graffiti artist [[Mare139]] is known for creating 3D sculptures of arrows.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Spiegel |first1=Ilyse |title=The History and Evolution of Arrows in Graffiti Art |url=https://panic39.com/en-gb/blogs/news/the-history-and-evolution-of-arrows-in-graffiti-art |website=panic39.com |date=22 May 2022}}</ref>

==Unicode==
